title: Supersolidophobic Pt catalyst for long-term natural seawater electrolysis with hydrogen production and magnesium extraction

paper_content.abstract: The electrochemical synthesis of solid compounds is a critical emerging area in electrocatalysis; however, a major challenge is still remaining on severe catalyst scaling driven by strong solid-solid interactions, giving rise to rapid electrode deactivation. In this study, for the example of simultaneous synthesis of Mg(OH)2 and H2 from natural seawater electrolysis, we demonstrate that Pt catalyst with surface-coordinated halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) can alleviate this scaling effect (i.e., solidophobicity) by like-charge repulsion and thus regulating the local environment. Specifically, Pt-I coordination results in supersolidophobicity, achieving a successful extraction of Mg(OH)2 (>99% purity) while stably producing H2 (under 100 mA cm-2 for over 5000 hours). A combination of experimental and theoretical studies reveals that, due to the like charge repulsion between I- and insitu generated OH-, the Pt-I catalyst regulates the surface pH gradient which increases the distance from the electrode surface to the Mg(OH)2 nucleus (>4 μm) and facilitates homogeneous nucleation. Additionally, the scalability of the Pt-I catalyst, along with the techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment of the natural seawater electrolysis technology are systematically demonstrated.
paper_content.introduction:
The production of green hydrogen fuel through water electrolysis is crucial for the advancement of renewable energy systems1–4. According to the World Energy Council, global hydrogen demand is projected to reach at least 148 million tons per year by 20505,6. However, compared to gray hydrogen, which is produced via methane reforming or coal gasification, the cost of green hydrogen production remains significantly higher (~US$2 and ~US$5 per kg H2 for gray and green hydrogen, respectively)7. In addition to the cost reduction of renewables, coupling water electrolysis with other value-increment reactions is considered an effective strategy to offset energy input costs8–10. The general approach involves replacing the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) with alternative anodic reactions that exhibit lower thermodynamic equilibrium potential and/or reduced kinetic overpotential11–13, such as electrooxidation of biomass molecules14, plastic wastes15, and organic compounds16. These alternatives have been extensively explored, achieving significant progress17–19. Another strategy is to capitalize on the surface alkaline environment generated in situ during the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at the cathode, which facilitates the extraction of valuable metal resources from the electrolyte by forming easily separable hydroxide precipitates. For instance, the electrolysis of natural seawater enriched with Mg2+ (>0.79 g/L) enables the simultaneous production of H2 and high-value Mg(OH)2 at the cathode20.

Although the aforementioned process elevates the benefits of seawater electrolysis, the severe adhesion of precipitates to the electrode surface, which leads to rapid electrode deactivation, limits its sustainability21–23. According to classical nucleation theory, heterogeneous nucleation on the electrode surface is thermodynamically more favorable than homogeneous nucleation due to the significantly lower nucleation energy barrier24,25. Therefore, from a kinetic perspective, it is essential to regulate the local reaction environment at the cathode during the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) to favor homogeneous nucleation of Mg(OH)2 in the electrolyte. However, the lack of in-depth studies on the local reaction environment significantly complicates solidophobic catalyst design26. In principle, the catalyst should simultaneously achieve high HER activity under near-neutral environment and exhibit solidophobic surface properties.

In this study, we demonstrate that the coordinated halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) on Pt catalysts are critical for regulating the local reaction environment while maintaining high HER activity. In experiments, the Pt-I catalyst loaded on a Ti substrate (Pt-I/Ti) exhibits the best solidophobic behavior (i.e., supersolidophobicity) and maintains stable operation at 100 mA cm−2 in natural seawater electrolyte for over 5000 h. In contrast, the unmodified Pt/Ti electrode is rapidly covered by Mg(OH)2, leading to a drastic degradation in current density (100 mA cm−2, <1 h, Fig. 1a). The stability of Pt-I/Ti is attributed to its ability to regulate the local surface reaction environment. This regulation arises from the like-charge repulsion between the surface halogen ligands and OH− generated during the HER process, which drives OH− away from the electrode and allows it to react with Mg2+ in the bulk seawater (Fig. 1b). In situ experiments and theoretical calculations indicate that surface-coordinated halogens remain stable throughout the HER process, with the peak OH− concentration occurring ~8 μm away from the surface, much farther than on an unmodified electrode (~3 μm). The practical applicability of this supersolidophobic electrode is demonstrated by assembling it in a scaled electrolyzer (electrode area: 100 cm2), which exhibits stable performance (10 A, >1000 h) for the simultaneous production of green H2 and Mg(OH)2 (5.54 g h−1, >99% purity). The double-product strategy contributes to reducing the H2 production cost and environmental impact in seawater electrolysis.
paper_content.results:
Preparation and characterization of the Pt-X/Ti (X: F, Cl, Br, I) electrocatalyst
The synthesis of Pt-X/Ti involves first electrodeposition of H2PtCl6 on Ti substrate to form Pt-Cl/Ti electrode, which is subsequently utilized to fabricate Pt-F/Ti, Pt-Br/Ti and Pt-I/Ti electrodes by exchanging the coordinated halogens, as schemed in Fig. 1a and Fig. S1 (details can be seen in Methods). The contrastive sample of Pt/Ti without coordinated halogens was also prepared, characterized and evaluated. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM), selected area electron diffraction (SAED) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) results of five samples exhibited negligible morphological differences of Pt and the same predominant exposed crystallographic plane (1, 1, 1) (Fig. S2-6), consistent with the samples obtained via electrodeposition methods reported previously27.

The energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) results of Pt-X/Ti from transmission electron microscopy (TEM) are shown in Fig. 2b–e, where the distributions of halogen elements align well with those of Pt. The results from ion chromatography and Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES) indicate that the four samples exhibit similar halogen/platinum content ratios (Fig. S7). Time of Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) was further employed to characterize the interaction between halogens and Pt nanoparticles28,29, as shown in Fig. 2f-i and Fig. S8. The 3D TOF-SIMS results demonstrated that PtX2- (X: F, Cl, Br, I) were primarily existed on the surface of four samples, while the concentrations gradually decreased with the increase of depth, directly proving that halogens coordinated with Pt were predominantly located at the surface. In contrast, negligible halogens can be detected on the surface of Pt nanoparticles for the Pt/Ti electrode without halogen-modification (Fig. S9).

Electrocatalytic performance in natural seawater
The HER activities of Pt/Ti, Pt-X/Ti (X: F, Cl, Br, I) and Pt foil were firstly evaluated in a standard three-electrode system with natural seawater (from Ningbo Bay after sediment removal, Fig. S10, 11, and Supplementary Table 1) as the electrolyte. As shown in Fig. 3a, the Pt-X/Ti required small overpotentials (445, 428, 450 and 465 mV for Pt-F/Ti, Pt-Cl/Ti, Pt-Br/Ti and Pt-I/Ti, respectively) for achieving industrial current density (~100 mA cm−2), better than those of Pt/Ti electrode and Pt foil (472 and 550 mV, respectively). The polarization curves without iR correction are presented in Fig. S13a. Moreover, the Tafel slope of Pt-X/Ti (163–196 mV dec−1) and the charge transfer resistance (3.4–9.5 Ω) further confirmed the advanced HER kinetics (Fig. S12b and 13, Supplementary Table 2)30–32. The enhanced HER activity can be explained by the enhanced first-electron-affinity due to surface coordinated halogens33. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations of the HER process in a neutral environment, as shown in Fig. S14, 15, reveal that the coordinated halogens weaken the adsorption energy of H* at adjacent Pt sites, thereby accelerating the Heyrovsky step and promoting the HER process34. The chlorine weaken the adsorption energy the most while iodine shows the weakest effect, consistent with the difference in HER activities.

Compared with HER activity, stability issue requires much more attention due to the severe scaling effect on electrode surface, resulting in fast electrode deactivation21,22,35,36. Thus, in order to screen the stabilities of different cathodes, the commercial boron-doped diamond (BDD) and 0.5 M Na2SO4 were adopted as anode and anolyte to ensure the stability of the anodic side, and the experiments were conducted in a three-electrode system equipped with a cation exchange membrane (Fig. S16, 17). Under the current density of 100 mA cm−2, the applied bias of Pt/Ti electrode without halogen-modification quickly increased ~100 mV within 30 min (Fig. 3b), which was majorly due to the decrease of working area caused by the coverage of white flocculent scale (Mg(OH)2, Fig. S18-20). In sharp contrast, all four Pt-X/Ti electrodes exhibited much enhanced stabilities under the same conditions. Specifically, Pt-F/Ti, Pt-Cl/Ti, and Pt-Br/Ti electrodes displayed potential increases of ~33 mV, ~29 mV, and ~17 mV, respectively, while Pt-I/Ti electrode maintained stable performance with negligible potential increase, demonstrating its supersolidophobic property. It is worth noting that, through comprehensive evaluation, the Pt-I/Ti electrode ranks among the first class for HER in natural seawater environment (Fig. S21, 22)37–40.

Meanwhile, optical images and XRD patterns of the four electrodes before and after the reaction further supported the difference in stabilities (Fig. S23, 24).

Benefiting from the simplicity of synthesis process, the Pt-I/Ti electrode can be easily scaled up to 100 cm2 in the laboratory, as shown in the inset of Fig. 3c and Fig. S25. The large-area consistency was demonstrated by selecting and evaluating, five different regions of the 100 cm2 electrode in terms of the HER activity and stability in natural seawater (Fig. 3c and Fig. S26). Moreover, as shown in Fig. 3e and Fig. S27-30, Micro X-ray Fluorescence (Micro-XRF) and SEM results revealed that most regions exhibited relatively identical elements distribution and morphology, further proving the scaling-up feasibility of this Pt-I/Ti electrode. More importantly, for practical application, the lifetime of the electrode is required at least thousands of hours (>1000 h)41,42. Therefore, in this case, we have extended the HER testing of Pt-I/Ti electrode in natural seawater over 5000 h and observed stable operation with a negligible increase in applied bias (<10 mV) (Fig. 3d and Fig. S31), which demonstrates competitive stability among the natural seawater cathodes reported previously (Supplementary Table 3)40,43–47.

The stability of Pt-I/Ti electrode heavily lies on the firmness of Pt-I coordination, which has been demonstrated in several ex situ and in situ characterizations. The Micro-XRF pattern of Pt-I/Ti electrode after 1000 h test demonstrated Pt and I elements maintain a uniform distribution. (Fig. 3e and Fig. S32, 33). As shown in Fig. 3f, the high-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra of I 3d for fresh and used Pt-I/Ti exhibited nearly identical peaks48,49, confirming the stable presence of coordinated iodine on Pt surface. The presence of coordinated halogens (F, Cl, Br) were also confirmed by the observation of ν(Pt-X, X: F, Cl, Br) peaks in Far-Infrared and XPS results (Fig. S34-36). In addition, in situ Raman spectroscopy revealed that, with the increase of applied bias from OCP to −1.0 V vs. RHE, the ν(Pt-I) remained detectable and unchanged at ~147 cm−150,51, while the δ(Pt-OH) at 1063 cm−1 did not appear at all33,52, as shown in Fig. 3g (experimental set-up is shown in the Fig. S37). This phenomenon demonstrates that the coordinated iodine is stable and cannot be replaced by the generated OH- during the HER process, and other halogens (F, Cl, Br) also show the same behavior (Fig. S37). The observable ν(S-O) peak at 980 cm−1 is attributed to the background signal from the electrolyte (Experimental details and Fig. S38).

Mechanistic investigation
Indeed, the synthesis of hydroxides on the electrode surface (i.e., Mg(OH)2 in this case) is closely related to the local reaction environment (i.e., pH) near the cathode during the HER process26,53. To further investigate the mechanism on how halogen coordination regulates the local reaction environment, a two-dimensional (2D) COMSOL Multiphysics model was firstly constructed to map out the pH distribution near the cathode surface (Fig. S39). It is found that the Pt/Ti electrode without halogen-modification exhibited a maximum pH value (~10.2) at ~3 μm from the electrode surface while the pH peak (~10.3) for the Pt-I/Ti electrode shifted to ~8 μm under a current density of 100 mA cm-2, as shown in Fig. 4a and Fig. S40. To verify this simulation, we developed a micro-region pH measurement system capable of in situ surface pH monitoring, and incorporated a stepper motor to measure the pH variation with distance (experimental set-up is shown in the Fig. S41). As shown in Fig. 4b and Fig. S42, the local pH of Pt/Ti electrode surface rapidly increased, achieving the minimum pH required for Mg(OH)2 precipitation (pH ≈ 9.6) at ~2 μm and complete precipitation (pH ≈ 11.1) at ~4 μm. In sharp contrast, for the Pt-I/Ti electrode, the pH reached 9.6 at ~4 μm and exceeded 11.1 at ~8 μm. These theoretical and experimental results both revealed that the surface diffusion of OH- was accelerated on the Pt-I/Ti electrodes, which were confirmed by other current densities (Fig. S43-45). It is worth noting that, for both electrodes, the maximum local pH during the HER process was lower than the minimum pH (~13.0) for starting the precipitation of Ca2+, giving rise to the potential in Ca-Mg separation from seawater. Further, open circuit potential (OCP) decay transients was used to verify interfacial pH swings during electrocatalysis54, and the results (Fig. 4c and Fig. S46, 47) demonstrated that the Pt-I/Ti electrode exhibited stronger resistance to pH increases which also indicated the accelerated OH- diffusion on electrode surface. It should be noted that the different OH- diffusion properties are consistent with *OH binding strength on Pt-X/Ti, as observed in the CO stripping experiments55,56, where Pt-I/Ti electrode exhibited the strongest repulsive capacity (Fig. S48).

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were used to validate the ion (e.g., Cl- or OH-) exclusion ability of the electrode surface57,58. The Pt and Pt-I slabs covered with solvent layers were constructed as model systems to explore the distribution of OH− close to the electrode surface (Fig. 4d, e, and Fig. S49). It is observed that the pure Pt surface would be surrounded by OH−, while the OH− ions on the Pt-I surface were repelled away from the surface. The number of OH− within 30 Å of the surface was halved (Fig. 4f), and the diffusion coefficients of OH- increased from 8.64 × 10−5 to 9.49 × 10−5 cm2 s−1 (Fig. S50).

Combined with the experimental and theoretical results, the HER process on electrode surfaces with or without halogen-modification in natural seawater can be illustrated in Figs. 4g, h. For the pure Pt surface, the diffusion of OH- generated by hydrogen evolution is dependent on the electrode repulsion and concentration gradient. Nevertheless, for the Pt-X surface, besides the above forces, like-charge repulsion from the halogen layer led to the faster OH- diffusion and expanded low-pH region. Thus, the combination of Mg2+ and OH- occurred closer to the pure Pt surface, which facilitated the heterogeneous nucleation process (i.e., Mg(OH)2 scaling). In contrast, for the Pt-X surface, as the position for Mg2+ precipitation was much farther from the electrode, homogeneous nucleation of Mg(OH)2 in the electrolyte was preferred (i.e., supersolidophobicity).

Performance and techno-economic analysis of scale electrolyzer
Compared with individual Mg2+ extraction and hydrogen production from seawater, this study achieves simultaneous production of H2 and high-purity Mg(OH)2 from seawater in virtue of the stable and supersolidophobic cathode (Fig. 5a). Next, the practical applicability of the supersolidophobic electrode was demonstrated in a large-scale direct seawater electrolyzer (electrode area: 100 cm2), assembled by a cation exchange membrane, an IrO2-Ti anode (Fig. S51-53), and a scaled Pt-I/Ti cathode, as schemed in Fig. 5b and Fig. S54-55. Natural seawater and 0.5 M Na2SO4 were used as the catholyte and anolyte, respectively. Fig. 5c demonstrated that the lab-made electrolyzer could be stably operated with a cell potential of ~2.75 V under 10 A for over 1000 h. During this process, the white Mg(OH)2 product was continuously produced at a rate of 5.54 g h−1, with a purity exceeding 99% and a particle size of ~35 μm (Fig. S56-61 and Supplementary Table 4). The catholyte pH was maintained at ~9.5 by flowing the natural seawater, resulting in a OH− availability of ~53.1% (Fig. S62). In contrast, for the traditional chemical precipitation method, the OH− availability was only ~16.7% when the solution pH was adjusted to ~9.6. With the pH increased further to ~11.0 by adding NaOH dropwise, the OH- availability rose to ~36.1%, although the purity of Mg(OH)2 ~91.4% (Fig. 5d, Fig. S63, 64, and Supplementary Table 5 and details can be seen in the Supplementary Discussion 1). The effective utilization of local pH indicates much enhanced OH− availability, which also represents a notable advantage of this value-increment natural seawater electrolysis strategy.

The TEA results were shown in Fig. 5e and Fig. S65, which summarized the preliminary and rough estimation of expenses associated with the direct conversion of natural seawater into valuable H2 and Mg(OH)2 (details can be seen in the Supplementary Discussion 2). The co-produced Mg(OH)2 could balance the hydrogen production cost, bringing the hydrogen production cost down to US$0.61 per kg of H2, which was below the DOE 2025 and 2030 targets (US$1.40 and US$1.00 per kg of H2, respectively)59–61 (Fig. S65). As shown in Fig. S66, 67, variations in each economic parameter from −10% to +10% of their original values produce linear trends with specific slopes. Compared to the original value, electricity cost shows a relatively smaller effect on hydrogen production costs. However, the slopes of the curves related to the prices of magnesium hydroxide and sodium hydroxide are steeper, indicating that any change in these parameters could have a significant impact on hydrogen production costs. We also conducted a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) to quantify its environmental impact compared to traditional hydrogen production processes (Fig. 5f, and Supplementary Table 6 and 7). In this assessment, the system expansion approach was adopted as the allocation method, assuming that the co-produced byproducts could equivalently replace the same quantities of conventionally produced materials in the market, thereby generating positive environmental benefits62. As shown in Fig. 5f, the process produces 8 t of O2 and 1.45 t of Mg(OH)2 along with 1 t of H2. Compared with average H2 production, the seawater electrolysis-based magnesium extraction and hydrogen production process reduces abiotic depletion potential (ADP) and global warming potential (GWP), while exhibiting higher values only in the ADP-element and ozone layer depletion potential (ODP) categories. The results indicate that this double-product strategy can reduce the overall environmental impact.

In summary, this study developed a series of halogen-modified Pt-X (X: F, Cl, Br, I) catalysts aiming at meeting the strict requirement (both high HER activity and solidophobic surface property) of cathode in natural seawater electrolysis. The supersolidophobic Pt-I/Ti cathode demonstrated stable performance for over 5000 h under 100 mA cm−2 in natural seawater electrolysis, while also enabling the co-electrosynthesis of high-purity Mg(OH)2 through the utilization of localized alkaline environment. Detailed characterizations, alongside COMSOL and classical MD simulations, revealed that the local reaction environment regulation and supersolidophobicity arise from the iodine modification on the electrode surface, inducing like-charge repulsion between I− and in situ generated OH- during the HER process and promoting homogeneous nucleation of solid product. Considering the high economic value of double-product advantage, the proposed seawater electrolysis strategy would reduce the sell price and environmental impact of green hydrogen. Furthermore, we can foresee that this strategy in constructing supersolidophobic electrode will be of significant important for future electro-synthesis of solid compounds.
paper_content.methods:
Chemicals
Chloroplatinic(IV) acid (H2PtCl6, Aladdin Industrial, ≥99.95%), potassium nitrate (KNO3, China National Pharmaceutical Group Corporation, ≥99.0%), sodium fluoride (NaF, Macklin reagent, 99.99%), sodium bromide (NaBr, Macklin reagent, 99.9%), sodium iodide (NaI, Macklin reagent, 99.9%), sodium sulfate (Na2SO4, Macklin reagent, ≥99.0%), sulfuric acid (H2SO4, China National Pharmaceutical Group Corporation, ≥96.0%), sodium hydroxide (NaOH, Aladdin Industrial, 97%), sodium phosphate dibasic (Na2HPO4, Aladdin Industrial, 99.9%), sodium dihydrogen phosphate (NaH2PO4, Aladdin Industrial, 99.9%), 5,5-Dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO, Aladdin Industrial, 97%). Ti mesh (99.5%, 100 mesh) and IrO2-Ti felt (thickness is 0.25 mm, loading amount: 2 mg cm−2) were purchased from Suzhou sinero technology Co., LTD. Carbon fiber paper (TGP-H-060, 0.19 mm) was purchased from TORAY Industries. Boron doped diamond (BDD) was purchased from Suzhou shure technology Co., LTD. Cation exchange membrane (Nafion 117, thickness is 183 μm) was purchased from Suzhou sinero technology Co., LTD. All deionized water was prepared with OmniaPure ultra-pure water system (resistivity of 18.2 MΩ). All chemical reagents were used as received without further purification.

Preparation of Ti mesh matrix electrode
First, the Ti mesh was cut into pieces with the size of 1 cm × 2 cm. Second, these pieces were sequentially degreased through sonication in acetone, ethanol, and deionized water for 10 min each. Subsequently, they were cleaned with 2 M H2SO4 in an ultrasound bath for 10 min to remove the surface impurity layer. Finally, the Ti mesh was washed with deionized water until attaining a neutral pH and dried at 60 °C for 3 h.

Preparation of Pt-Cl/Ti electrode
The Pt-Cl/Ti electrode was synthesized through electrochemical deposition strategy in the three-electrode system, wherein the Ti mesh, graphite paper and saturated calomel electrode (SCE) electrode served as the working electrode, counter electrode, and reference electrode, respectively. The electrodeposition solution contained 0.0015 M H2PtCl6 and 0.1 M KNO3. The Pt-Cl/Ti was prepared using the i-t method at a potential of −0.3 V for 15 min, followed by washed with deionized water and dried at 60 °C for 3 h. Pt loading amount: Pt-Cl/Ti (0.254 mg cm-2).

Preparation of Pt-X/Ti (X: F, Br, I) electrodes by coordination exchange
The Cl ligand can be removed under the irradiation of visible light in water. CEL-HXUV300E from China Education Au-light with a spectral region from 320 nm to 780 nm was used as the light source with an output power density of 3.75 mW cm−2. After 30 min of irradiation, the electrode was immersed in 2 M NaX (X: F, Br, I) at 40 °C for 4 h under magnetic stirring. Finally, the Pt-X/Ti (X: F, Br, I) electrode was washed with deionized water and dried at 60 °C for 3 h. Pt loading amount: Pt-F/Ti (0.253 mg cm−2), Pt-Br/Ti (0.248 mg cm−2) and Pt-I/Ti (0.247 mg cm−2).

Preparation of Pt/Ti electrode
The Pt/Ti electrode was synthesized by calcining the Pt-Cl/Ti electrode in a tube furnace with a 5% H2/Ar flow under 200 °C for 4 h. Pt loading amount: Pt/Ti (0.248 mg cm−2).

Preparation of Pt-X/CFP (X: F, Cl, Br, I) and Pt/CFP electrodes
The synthesis method for the Pt-X/CFP (X: F, Cl, Br, I) and Pt/CFP electrodes is similar to that for the Pt-X/Ti (X: F, Cl, Br, I) and Pt/Ti electrodes, with the only difference being the substitution of the substrate with carbon fiber paper.

Preparation of scaled Pt-I/Ti electrode
The synthesis procedure of scaled Pt-I/Ti electrode is similar to that of the 1 cm × 2 cm Pt-I/Ti electrode, with the only difference being the substitution of the Ti matrix (10 cm × 10 cm). The electrode was then electrodeposited using a laboratory-made electrodepositing cell for 20 min, followed by washing with deionized water and drying at 60 °C for 3 h.

Seawater Pretreatment
Seawater pretreatment only sediment removal by filtration system (filter paper diameter = 150 mm).

Material characterizations
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were taken on Hitachi S4800 working at 20 keV. The aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM measurements were taken on a JEM-ARM200F instrument at 200 keV. The crystal structures of the samples were examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D8) with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.154178 nm). The surface structures of Pt-X/Ti (X: F, Cl, Br, I) electrodes were analyzed by PHI nanoTOF II TOF-SIMS (ULVAC-PHI, Japan). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were performed by using a Thermo ESCALAB 250 high-performance electron spectrometer using monochromatized Al Ka (hν = 1486.6 eV) as the excitation source. Raman measurements were conducted by using a RENISHAW inVia Raman spectrometer. Far-Infrared spectra were obtained on a Bruker Vertex 70V. The content of cations in seawater was measured by Agilent ICP 720 inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES). Micro X-ray Fluorescence (Micro-XRF) images were taken on a Bruker M4 TORNADO. The product particle size was measured by Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS90. Faradaic efficiencies were tested by using gas chromatography (GC, Agilent 7890B) method30. The electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra were collected on a Bruker Elexsys 500 spectrometer at 25 °C. Micro-region pH measurements were performed by using a commercial glass-type pH microelectrode with a tip diameter of 500 μm (Unisense, pH-500c), together with an internal reference.

Electrochemical measurements
Except for the electrolyzer stabilization process, all of the electrochemical measurements were measured on electrochemical workstation (ChenHua CH instrument 760E) with a three-electrode configuration at 25 °C. Except in stability tests, the fabricated samples, graphite paper and saturated calomel electrode (SCE, saturated KCl) served as the working electrode, counter electrode, and reference electrode, respectively. In a stability test, the fabricated samples, commercial boron-doped diamond (BDD, 3 cm × 4 cm) and saturated calomel electrode (SCE, saturated KCl) acted as the reference electrode, counter electrode, and reference electrode, respectively. The as-fabricated electrodes were clamped by pure Ti holder (100%) to make electrical contact. The electrolyte (100 mL natural seawater, pH = 7.71 ± 0.02 and 100 mL 0.5 M Na2SO4, pH = 7.0 ± 0.02) was purged with pure N2 (for HER) or O2 (for OER) for at least 30 min. The polarization curves of HER were documented at a rate of 5 mV s−1. LSV is measured independently three times.

The reference electrodes were calibrated in an electrolyte saturated with high-purity hydrogen, using two platinum foils (1 × 1 cm2) as the working and counter electrodes, respectively. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1. The thermodynamic potential of the hydrogen electrode reaction was determined as the average of the two potentials at which the current crossed zero during the CV scans, and this value was used to convert the measured potentials to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). All potentials of the measured curves were corrected with iR (100%)63 compensation and then converted to RHE according to the following two equations:

E(RHE) = E(Ag/AgCl) + 0.0592 × pH + 0.1989 (1)

E(RHE) = E(SCE) + 0.0592 × pH + 0.2440 (2)

The service life of the electrodes in the electrolyzer was tested using a direct current (DC) power supply (MAISHENG, MP1560D) with a constant current density in a two-electrode mode, and the cell potential was recorded every hour, commercial IrO2-Ti (10 cm × 10 cm) acted as the counter electrode. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) curves were obtained by a frequency range from 1000 kHz to 0.1 Hz under different potentials.

All the solutions used as electrolytes are prepared freshly and used immediately, and are stored in a dark place.

MEA measurement
The MEA setup with the geometric area of 100 cm2 was designed and manufactured by the lab and equipped with a designed flow channel. The as prepared electrodes (Pt-I/Ti, 10 cm × 10 cm) and commercial IrO2-Ti felt (10 cm × 10 cm) electrode were selected as HER and OER electrodes, respectively. The cation exchange membrane was Nafion 117 (Dupont, USA). The membranes were pretreated by boiling sequentially in 3% H2O2 solution for 1 h and 0.5 M H2SO4 for 3 h, followed by rinsing in deionized water. The stability was carried out on DC power supply. The anolyte (0.5 M Na2SO4, 20 L) and catholyte (natural seawater, 20 L) were replaced every 6 h to maintain a constant pH, with the cathode effluent pH consistently stabilized at ~9.5.

Electrochemical in situ Raman measurements
Electrochemical in situ Raman spectroscopy was carried out using a RENISHAW inVia Raman spectrometer equipped with a Leica TCS SP8 CARS microscope and a Spectra-Physics 532 nm Ar laser. All in situ Raman measurements were performed with a custom-made spectro-electrochemical cell. The electrochemical activities were measured in a three-electrode configuration at 25 °C. The as prepared electrodes, Pt wire and Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) electrode served as the working electrode, counter electrode, and reference electrode, respectively. The electrolytes were 0.5 M Na2SO4. Noted that, to prevent side reactions, a sulfate solution is used. The laser beams were focused on the sample through the quartz window to collect the Raman spectrum. The chronoamperometry method was employed to applied different potentials to the electrode with 100 mV intervals in the range of 0 V to −1.0 V vs. RHE. The acquisition time for each spectrum was 10 s with 3 sweeps from 100.92 to 1811.54 cm−1. The optical images of custom-built electrochemical cells for in situ Raman measurements is provided in Supplementary Fig. 37.

CO stripping measurements
The CO stripping experiment was performed in a three-electrode H-cell configuration. The system employed a graphite rod as the counter electrode, a saturated calomel electrode (SCE, saturated KCl) as the reference electrode, and the as-prepared electrode as the working electrode. Initially, 10% CO/Ar gas was introduced into a CO-saturated 0.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte, allowing CO adsorption onto the working electrode at a constant potential of 0.1 V (vs. RHE) for 30 min. Subsequently, the electrode was transferred to an Ar-saturated 0.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte for CV analysis. Prior to measurement, the solution was purged with Ar gas, and CO stripping CV curves were recorded at a scan rate of 20 mV s−1.

Micro-region pH measurements
To test the pH on the electrode surface, a laboratory-made micro-region pH system equipped with a microscope (ZOOM-650, Shenzhen MicroVision Technology Co., Ltd.) and a stepper motor was used to measure pH variation with distance (Marzhauser Wetzlar MM33 with tilting device, step size: 1 μm). The electrolyte was 0.5 M Na2SO4, and the as prepared electrodes, Pt foil, and saturated calomel electrode (SCE, saturated KCl) served as the working electrode, counter electrode, and reference electrode, respectively. Initially, the glass-type pH microelectrode tip (Unisense, pH-500c) was positioned ~1 μm from the electrode surface using the stepper motor. A constant current was then applied, and the pH electrode was controlled to move away from the electrode surface in 1 μm increments. At each test point, the pH electrode was held for 1 s before moving to the next point. Each set of measurements was repeated three times to minimize error. The optical image of custom-built system for micro-region pH measurements is provided in Supplementary Fig. 41.

Open circuit potential (OCP) decay transients measurements
The open circuit potential (OCP) decay transients can be used to verify interfacial pH swings during electrocatalysis54. The electrolyte was 100 mL 0.5 M NaPi (Phosphate buffer, pH = 6.8 ± 0.02), and the as prepared electrodes, Pt foil, and saturated calomel electrode (SCE, saturated KCl) served as the working electrode, counter electrode, and reference electrode, respectively. Multi-step chronopotentiometry (CP) was employed to galvanostatically polarize the working electrode at current densities of 10, 25, 50 and 100 mA cm−2 for 2 min, with a data collection interval of 0.25 s, allowing a steady-state potential to be reached. Subsequently, a second CP step at the same current density, but with a higher data collection interval of 0.0002 s, was performed for 1 second. A third CP step at 0 mA cm−2 was used to collect the open circuit potential decay transient with a data collection interval of 0.0002 s for 1 s. Finally, a fourth CP step at 0 mA cm−2, with a lower data collection interval of 0.25 s, was conducted to capture the remainder of the open circuit potential decay. The data collection intervals were carefully selected to ensure high timer resolution during the termination of polarization, while avoiding the data buffering capacities of the potentiostat.

Theoretical computation details
All density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) with the projector augmented-wave (PAW) method64. The exchange-correlation interactions were described using the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional. A plane-wave energy cutoff of 450 eV was employed, and partial occupancies of the Kohn-Sham orbitals were treated using the Gaussian smearing method with a width of 0.2 eV. The self-consistent calculations apply a convergence energy threshold of 10−5 eV, and the force convergency was set to 0.05 eV Å−1. The p(3 × 3) Pt(111) surface was built with 4 layers, where two of the layers at the bottom was fixed in all the calculations. The coordinated halogen atoms (F, Cl, Br, I) was adsorbed on the top site of Pt, and the relevant affected site for HER was considered closed to the adsorbed halogen atoms. The k-point of 3 × 3 × 1 was used. The reaction free energy of H+ involved steps was calculated following the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model65. Free energy corrections were considered at the temperature of 298 K, following:

ΔG = ΔE + ΔGZPE + ΔGU - TΔS (3)

Here, ΔE, ΔGZPE, ΔGU, and ΔS represent the DFT-calculated energy change, the zero-point energy correction, the internal energy correction, and the entropy correction, respectively66.

All Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations were applied to calculation the number distribution and diffusion coefficients of OH− in seawater at pristine Pt (111) and I− adsorbed Pt (111) surfaces under an external electric field of 0.2 V Å−1 along z direction. The solid–liquid interface calculations were conducted with COMPASS III force field using the Forcite module in Materials Studio (MS) 2020. The dimensional lengths of the Pt substrate are 24.89 Å × 23.95 Å in xoy plane, which is composed of four layer Pt atoms. The solution contains 24 OH−, 36 Na+, 2 Mg2+, 16 Cl− and 1200 H2O molecules in a rectangular box with length scales of 24.89 Å × 23.95 Å × 61.86 Å. After geometry optimization, the aqueous solution was placed on pristine Pt (111) and I− adsorbed Pt (111) surfaces. All MD calculations were performed under the NVT ensemble (T = 298.0 K) with a timestep of 1 fs and a total simulation time of 400 ps, during which simulation trajectories were recorded every 4000 steps. The running time was long enough for system energy and temperature reaching stable. The temperature was controlling by a Nose–Hoover thermostat. The Ewald scheme and atom-based cutoff method (i.e., a radius of 12.5 Å) were applied to treat electrostatic and van der Waals (vdW) interactions, respectively. The number profiles of OH− along perpendicular direction were analyzed. The solid–liquid interfaces snapshots were displayed. The diffusion coefficients of OH− can be estimated from the slope of the mean square displacement (MSD) curves by the Einstein relationship.

The atomic coordinates of the optimized crystal structures can be found in Supplementary Data 1.

LCA analysis
An LCA was conducted using the SimaPro software following the international standard ISO 14040. The CML 2001 method was selected to evaluate the environmental impacts of the studied system, and background data were obtained from the Ecoinvent 3.11 database. The production of 1 t of hydrogen was defined as the functional unit, and the system boundary was set on a cradle-to-gate basis, covering the production processes of hydrogen and magnesium hydroxide in the seawater electrolysis-based magnesium extraction and hydrogen production process. A life-cycle inventory was established to clearly distinguish the system inputs and outputs. The main inputs include seawater, sodium hydroxide, catalyst materials, and electricity, while the outputs consist of hydrogen, oxygen, and magnesium hydroxide. A system expansion approach was applied for the attributional LCA, assuming that the co-produced byproducts could substitute conventionally produced materials in the market and thereby generate environmental benefits. Based on the CML 2001 method, the characterization analysis quantified the specific contributions of each environmental impact category (AP, GWP, FAETP, MAETP, TETP, ADP, EP, HTP, ADP element, ODP, and POCP) to represent the overall life-cycle environmental impacts.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript addresses the modification of a Pt catalyst with halogens to suppress Mg(OH)₂ deposition on the electrode surface via OH⁻ repulsion. This work builds upon the authors' previous publications in the field (e.g., https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c01484). Here, the authors demonstrate excellent long-term stability and scalability of the catalyst. I would say the manuscript can be recommended for publication. However, I have several suggestions for improvement:
1. The term supersolidophobic is not clearly defined in the existing literature. It remains unclear why the system is referred to as supersolidophobic compared to the authors’ prior “solidophobic” reports. A clearer definition and distinction are needed.
2. The procedure for preparing Pt-halogen electrodes via light irradiation and treatment with NaX solutions is insufficiently explained. If Pt electrodes can be modified in seawater containing halides, what prevents similar modifications from occurring naturally? Furthermore, the pure Pt/Ti electrode is calcined at 200 °C, but this is not mentioned for halogen-modified electrodes. For consistency, the preparation protocol should be the same or explicitly justified. If light treatment significantly alters the surface, the appropriate reference should be the light-treated Pt/Ti electrode.
3. What happens when the electrodes are tested in deionized or distilled water? Is the enhanced efficiency of halogen-modified electrodes still observed, or is it specific to seawater?
4. The proposed repulsion between I⁻ and OH⁻ is plausible, but in real seawater, halogens may undergo redox reactions or ion exchange. To support the stability of halogen coordination, I recommend complementing micro-XRF with ICP analysis of the electrolyte before and after electrolysis to track halogen leaching and quantify surface species.
5. The focus is largely on halogen content, but little is said about the oxidation states of Pt. Halogen coordination should affect Pt’s electronic environment, which can be detected via XPS. The manuscript should include quantification of halogen-to-metal ratios and discuss electronic effects on Pt: how much is in reduced state and oxidized...
6. The reported shift in the pH gradient from 3 μm to 8 μm is interesting, but the spatial and temporal resolution of the measurement is not described. Clarifying the method’s resolution and limitations is essential for evaluating the significance of this observation.
7. The HER activity of Pt-I is slightly lower than Pt-Cl or Pt-F, yet Pt-I is the chosen system. The rationale behind this choice —possibly superior solidophobicity or long-term performance—should be better justified.
8. While Faradaic efficiency for H₂ is reported to be near 100%, there is no mention of Mg(OH)₂ or O₂ balances. Additionally, what happens to the residual chloride ions after Mg precipitation?
9. Could the accumulation or partial passage of Mg(OH)₂ impact membrane performance over time? This possibility should be addressed or ruled out experimentally.
10. How does this system compare with commercial seawater electrolysis technologies in terms of cost, durability, and performance metrics? Including such a benchmark would enhance the manuscript's relevance to applied research.
11. The statement that this system “outperforms” previously reported seawater cathodes may be overstated. Some of the cited systems were tested for shorter durations, which does not necessarily imply inferior performance.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In the manuscript entitled “Supersolidophobic Pt catalyst for long-term natural seawater electrolysis with high-purity magnesium extraction”, Lu and co-workers present a Pt catalyst with surface-coordinated halogens (e.g., F, Cl, Br, I) which can promote like-charge repulsion mechanism to achieve a successful extraction of high-purity Mg(OH)2 with the stable green H2 production from seawater. The manuscript presents innovative research methods and promising preliminary results. However, it requires minor revisions to address several points before it can be considered for publication. Below are detailed comments and suggestions:
1. The authors should ensure numerical consistency throughout the manuscript. For instance, the purity of Mg(OH)2 is stated as 99.0% in the main text but appears as 99% in Figure 5. Which value is correct? Similarly, the Mg(OH)2 production rate is given as 5.54 g h-1 (two significant figures) in the main text, but the corresponding balance data in Supplementary Figure 54 appears to show only one significant figure. Please verify and correct these discrepancies.
2. The provided 3D TOF-SIMS images indicate that Pt-Br/Ti exhibits the most abundant PtBr2⁻ signal, surpassing that of the Pt-Cl/Ti precursor. This finding is somewhat confusing, given that Pt-X/Ti (F, Br, I) samples are synthesized via halogen exchange from Pt-Cl/Ti; one might expect similar PtX2⁻ abundances across these samples. The EDX data shows a similar trend. However, Supplementary Figure 34 (XPS) reveals a much weaker Cl signal compared to F and Br. The authors should clarify this apparent contradiction between the TOF-SIMS/EDX and XPS results regarding halogen abundance/distribution.
3. To robustly support the claim of Pt-X coordination (beyond physical adsorption), additional characterizations such as comparative XPS analysis should be provided. Specifically, comparing the binding energies of Pt and relevant halogens in the catalyst samples with those of bare Pt and PtX2 reference compounds would be highly informative to demonstrate chemical shifts indicative of coordination.
4. There appears to be an error in Supplementary Figure 12: the y-axis should be labeled "-Z’’" instead of "Z’’". Additionally, the axes scales should be consistent across the relevant panels. Please correct this figure.
5. The authors selected Ti felt as the catalyst substrate. Could the rationale for not using potentially cheaper alternatives, such as carbon fiber paper, be briefly discussed? Are there specific stability or performance considerations favoring Ti felt in this seawater electrolysis system?
6. Additional characterization of the produced Mg(OH)2, such as TEM imaging to examine its morphology and crystallinity, would strengthen the analysis of the extraction product.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This study presents a novel platinum (Pt) catalyst modified with surface-coordinated halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) for long-term natural seawater electrolysis, enabling simultaneous high-purity Mg(OH)₂ extraction and green hydrogen production. The Pt–I/Ti cathode exhibits supersolidophobicity, attributed to like-charge repulsion between iodide (I⁻) ions and in situ-generated hydroxide (OH⁻) ions. This repulsion shifts Mg(OH)₂ nucleation away from the electrode surface, promoting homogeneous rather than heterogeneous nucleation. As a result, the system achieves outstanding operational stability (>5,000 hours at 100 mA cm⁻²), yields high-purity Mg(OH)₂, and reduces hydrogen production costs to $0.52/kg—outperforming U.S. DOE targets. Overall, this work is highly innovative and suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
Regarding the molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, I have a few comments to provide more simulation details:
1. Figure 4d–f demonstrates that OH⁻ ions are repelled from the Pt–I surface but accumulate near pristine Pt. Which specific intermolecular interactions or force field parameters in the COMPASS III model (as detailed in the Supplementary Methods) are responsible for the electrostatic repulsion between surface-bound iodide (I⁻) and OH⁻ ions?
2. The MD system (Supplementary Figure 47) contains 24 OH⁻, 36 Na⁺, 2 Mg²⁺, 16 Cl⁻, and 1,200 H₂O molecules. What was the rationale behind selecting these specific ion concentrations?
3. Figure 4f shows that the number of OH⁻ ions within 30 Å of the Pt–I surface is approximately half that near pristine Pt. How was this spatial distribution of OH⁻ ions quantified—e.g., using radial distribution functions (RDFs)?
4. The MD simulations applied an external electric field of 0.2 V/Å along the z-direction (as described in the Supplementary Information). How was this field strength chosen, and does it reflect the experimental electrolysis conditions?
5. Were MD simulations also conducted for other halogen-modified surfaces (Pt–F, Pt–Cl, Pt–Br)? If so, how did their OH⁻ exclusion behaviors compare with Pt–I? If not, could the trend in halogen electronegativity (F > Cl > Br > I) provide mechanistic insight into the unique supersolidophobicity observed for Pt–I?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
Dear authors,
First of all, I would like to congratulate you on your insightful work concerning the ‘Supersolidophobic Pt catalyst for long-term natural seawater electrolysis with high-purity magnesium extraction’. The paper addresses the challenge of catalyst deactivation innovatively, while simultaneously pursuing the ‘double-product strategy’ of producing both green and cheap hydrogen and high-purity Mg(OH)2. The manuscript is high of quality and very well written. Besides, the techno-economic assessment and its details in the supplementary information are very well explained and followed an understandable order.
I have several points of suggestion to be considered to improve the quality of the manuscript and increase the robustness of your outcomes. These suggested points will improve the quality of your assessments and will benefit the visibility of your work:
MAIN TEXT:
•Line 1-2: Title
o The main focus of the paper is the double-product strategy to produce green/sustainable hydrogen and high-purity magnesium. However, in the title, hydrogen is not mentioned. Consider adding hydrogen as well. By doing so, you will increase your visibility.

o Make sure that the figures are readable in the article. Or consider restructuring to improve readability and visibility.

o Fig. 5e: Make the benefits of Mg(OH)2 better visible.

o Discussion point based on the sensitivity assessment in the Supplementary Information (SI) (see SI part below).

o Based on your explanation to keep the pH of the anolyte stabilized, you need to add NaOH, which tells me that OH is depleting (due to OH- usage) and Na is increasing in the seawater that is potentially released into the sea again? Response to Reviewer 1
General Comment: The manuscript addresses the modification of a Pt catalyst with
halogens to suppress Mg(OH) deposition on the electrode surface via OH- repulsion.
https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c01484). Here, the authors
demonstrate excellent long-term stability and scalability of the catalyst. I would say the
manuscript can be recommended for publication. However, I have several suggestions
for improvement:
Response: We do appreciate the reviewer’s attention to our previous work and the
positive comments provided; the point-by-point response is shown below.
Comment 1: The term supersolidophobic is not clearly defined in the existing literature.
It remains unclear why the system is referred to as supersolidophobic compared to the
authors’ prior “solidophobic” reports. A clearer definition and distinction are needed.
Response: The term “supersolidophobic” is derived from superhydrophobicity and
superaerophobic1,2, referring to the suppression of solid detachment and adsorption on
the surface of other material surface. In our previous work, we introduced the concept
of solidophobic properties; however, the stability of the electrode remained to be
improved3. In this manuscript, we have demonstrated the enhanced stability of the
electrode, and therefore, we refer to it as “supersolidophobic”, indicating a material that
simultaneously exhibits solidophobic properties along with unprecedented long-term
stability and high durability.
Comment 2: The procedure for preparing Pt-halogen electrodes via light irradiation
and treatment with NaX solutions is insufficiently explained. If Pt electrodes can be
modified in seawater containing halides, what prevents similar modifications from
occurring naturally? Furthermore, the pure Pt/Ti electrode is calcined at 200 °C, but
this is not mentioned for halogen-modified electrodes. For consistency, the preparation
protocol should be the same or explicitly justified. If light treatment significantly alters
the surface, the appropriate reference should be the light-treated Pt/Ti electrode.
Response: During the halogen coordination exchange process, the first step involves
the removal of Cl- from the Pt-Cl/Ti. In this process, light exposure is essential4-6; this
reaction does not occur in the absence of light. Subsequently, halogen exchange (F, Br,
I) takes place. The reaction cannot occur under the reaction conditions without the
necessary light exposure. The calcination process at 200°C and reduction atmosphere
aims to obtain a non-coordinated Pt/Ti electrode, which serves as a comparison sample
to demonstrate the role of halogen coordination. To confirm that calcination does not
induce other effects on the sample, we performed thermal treatment on Pt-I/Ti in a N
2
atmosphere. As shown in Figure R1a, the calcined Pt-I/Ti sample requires an
overpotential of 450 mV to reach 100 mA cm-2, which is almost identical to the value
before calcination (465 mV). Under a current density of 100 mA cm-2, the applied bias
of the calcined Pt-I/Ti sample remains consistent with that before calcination (Figure
R1b). Additionally, we conducted light exposure treatment on the Pt/Ti sample, and the
treated sample exhibited almost the same behavior as the initial sample (Figure R2).
Figure R1. (a) Polarization curves with iR correction of Pt-I/Ti and Pt-I/Ti after
calcination in natural seawater (pH=7.71). (b) Short-term durability test of Pt-I/Ti and
Pt-I/Ti after calcination in natural seawater electrolysis under 100 mA cm-2.
Figure R2. (a) Polarization curves with iR correction of Pt/Ti and Pt/Ti after light
treatment in natural seawater (pH=7.71). (b) Short-term durability test of Pt/Ti and Pt/Ti
after light treatment in natural seawater electrolysis under 100 mA cm-2.
Comment 3: What happens when the electrodes are tested in deionized or distilled
water? Is the enhanced efficiency of halogen-modified electrodes still observed, or is it
specific to seawater?
Response: The enhancement of platinum site activity by halogen modification is
attributed to the reduction of the adsorption energies of H* on the platinum active sites7,
making it applicable in various solution environments6. As shown in Figure R3, LSV
testing was conducted in 0.5 M Na SO , and the Pt-X/Ti electrodes still required small
2 4
overpotentials (458, 428, 465, and 474 mV for Pt-F/Ti, Pt-Cl/Ti, Pt-Br/Ti, and Pt-I/Ti,
respectively) to achieve the industrial current density (~100 mA cm-2), outperforming
the Pt/Ti electrode (488 mV).
Figure R3. Polarization curves with iR correction of Pt/Ti and Pt-X/Ti in 0.5 M Na SO
2 4
(pH=7).
Comment 4: The proposed repulsion between I⁻ and OH⁻ is plausible, but in real
seawater, halogens may undergo redox reactions or ion exchange. To support the
stability of halogen coordination, I recommend complementing micro-XRF with ICP
analysis of the electrolyte before and after electrolysis to track halogen leaching and
quantify surface species.
Response: To verify the stability of halogen coordination before and after the reaction,
we conducted a 100 h electrolysis test (Figure R4) with samples taken at different time
points for analysis. As shown in Figure R5, the iodine content in the solution remained
consistently below the detection limit of ion chromatography, indicating that the Pt-I
coordination remained stable throughout the reaction process, with negligible I-
leaching.
Figure R4. Stability tests of Pt-I/Ti electrode under 100 mA cm-2.
Figure R5. The raw data of Pt-I/Ti from ion chromatography during the stability tests.
(a) 0 h, (b) 5 h, (c) 20 h, (d) 50 h, (e) 75 h and (f) 100 h.
Note: The choice of using Na SO as the electrolyte was made because, when
2 4
circulating natural seawater is used as the electrolyte, the renewal of the electrolyte may
result in a low concentration of leached ions, making detection difficult. Therefore,
Na SO was used as the electrolyte, and circulation was eliminated to investigate
2 4
possible ion leaching during the reaction. Trace amounts of Cl- originated from the
Na SO (Macklin reagent, 99.95%) used.
2 4
Comment 5: The focus is largely on halogen content, but little is said about the
oxidation states of Pt. Halogen coordination should affect Pt’s electronic environment,
which can be detected via XPS. The manuscript should include quantification of
halogen-to-metal ratios and discuss electronic effects on Pt: how much is in reduced
state and oxidized.
Response: Halogen coordination with platinum induces electron transfer from
platinum to the halogen8. The 4f peaks of Pt in the Pt-F/Ti, Pt-Cl/Ti, Pt-Br/Ti, and Pt-
7/2
I/Ti samples are located between Pt2+ (72.7 eV) and Pt4+ (74.9 eV) (Figure R6),
indicating that the average valence states of these platinum species range between +2
and +49. To quantitatively analyze the halogen-to-platinum ratio, we dissolved the
electrode samples with different halogen coordination and performed ion
chromatography and ICP-OES tests. As shown in Figure R7, the ratios of halogen to
platinum are close and Cl/Pt ratio is the highest , indicating that some loss occurs during
the halogen exchange process.
Figure R6. High-resolution XPS spectra of Pt 4f for (a) Pt/Ti, (b) Pt-F/Ti, (c) Pt-Cl/Ti,
(d) Pt-Br/Ti and (e) Pt-I/Ti. (f) Binding energy of Pt 4f .
7/2
Note: The effect of fluorine on platinum is smaller than that of chlorine because the
electron affinity of fluorine is lower than that of chlorine, making it more difficult for
platinum to transfer electrons to fluorine.
Figure R7. The ratio of platinum to halogen in different samples.
Revision in the revised Supplementary Information (Figure 7 and 36):

F/Ti, (c) Pt-Cl/Ti, (d) Pt-Br/Ti and (e) Pt-I/Ti. (f) Binding energy of Pt 4f .

Note: The effect of fluorine on platinum is smaller than that of chlorine because the

Comment 6: The reported shift in the pH gradient from 3 μm to 8 μm is interesting, but
the spatial and temporal resolution of the measurement is not described. Clarifying the
method’s resolution and limitations is essential for evaluating the significance of this
observation.
Response: Due to the limitations of existing technologies, such as stepper motors and
microscopes, the minimum spatial resolution for micro-region pH testing is 1 μm, with
a minimum pH accuracy of 0.01 and a single-point response time of 1 s. In the future,
we plan to further develop a micro-region pH 3D testing system to enable more precise
analysis of pH variations on the material surface during catalytic reactions. We are sorry
that the test is not such precise, thanks for your understanding!
Comment 7: The HER activity of Pt-I is slightly lower than Pt-Cl or Pt-F, yet Pt-I is
the chosen system. The rationale behind this choice—possibly superior solidophobicity
or long-term performance—should be better justified.
Response: Stability is a crucial issue for seawater electrolysis for hydrogen
production10-12. To meet the demands of future industrial applications, electrodes must
exhibit a very high stablity13,14, especially in seawater electrolysis with hydrogen
production and magnesium extraction. The degradation of electrode performance in this
system primarily results from the adhesion of Mg(OH) , which negatively impacts the
2
overall system. Therefore, we selected the Pt-I/Ti electrode, which demonstrates the
highest stability. Notably, as shown in Figure R8, after 0.5 hour of reaction, the
overpotential of Pt-I/Ti at 100 mA cm-2 (436 mV) is superior to that of other halogen-
coordinated electrodes.
Figure R8. Short-term durability test of Pt/Ti and Pt-X/Ti in natural seawater
electrolysis under 100 mA cm-2.
Comment 8: While Faradaic efficiency for H₂ is reported to be near 100%, there is no
mention of Mg(OH)₂ or O₂ balances. Additionally, what happens to the residual
chloride ions after Mg precipitation?
Response: Faradaic efficiency for gas generation during the reaction was measured
using gas chromatography (GC). As shown in Figure R9, the oxygen generation
Faradaic efficiency (FE) of Pt-I/Ti in a three-electrode system in 0.5 M Na SO is close
2 4
to 100%. The conversion efficiency of magnesium hydroxide reflects the utilization of
OH-, which in the natural seawater electrolysis system is 53.1% (Figure R10). During
electrolysis, as magnesium ions precipitate, Na+ in the anode region is transported to
the cathode region through the ion-exchange membrane under the influence of diffusion
and electric field forces. This results in an increase in the NaCl concentration in the

Comment 1: Figure 4d–f demonstrates that OH⁻ ions are repelled from the Pt–I
surface but accumulate near pristine Pt. Which specific intermolecular interactions or

Response: The COMPASS III force field (Supplementary Methods) was used to
analyze the interactions between I- and OH-, which explicitly include: (i) Coulombic
interactions (electrostatic repulsion) between charged species; and (ii) van der Waals
(vdW) interactions (Lennard–Jones potential). Since both are anions, electrostatic
repulsion dominates, resulting in fewer OH- on the Pt-I surface.
Charge distribution: (i) Iodine (I-) adsorbed on Pt was modeled as a point charge
(q=-1eq=-1e) based on its anionic state; (ii) OH- was similarly assigned q=-1eq=-1e.
Key parameter: The repulsive force between I- and OH- follows Coulomb’s
law:𝐹 = 𝑘 𝑞1𝑞2, where q , q are negative charges of I- and OH-, respectively, and 𝑟 is
e 𝑟2 1 2
their separation distance. The specific force field parameters were automatically
assigned to I- and OH- by the Forcite module in the COMPASS III software.
Comment 2: The MD system (Supplementary Figure 47) contains 24 OH⁻, 36 Na⁺, 2
Mg²⁺, 16 Cl⁻, and 1,200 H₂O molecules. What was the rationale behind selecting these
specific ion concentrations?
Response: In the MD system, the number of ions was determined to reflect the real
conditions during the reaction. The OH- concentration was elevated to model the locally
alkaline environment during hydrogen evolution reaction (pH≈13.0). The amounts of
Na⁺, Mg2⁺, and Cl- were set close to their levels in seawater to maintain electroneutrality.
Consequently, the ion ratios approximate those of seawater (Supplementary Table 1),
while OH- was amplified to account for in situ generation during HER.
Comment 3: Figure 4f shows that the number of OH⁻ ions within 30 Å of the Pt–I
surface is approximately half that near pristine Pt. How was this spatial distribution of
OH⁻ ions quantified—e.g., using radial distribution functions (RDFs)?
Response: The number of OH- was quantified not by using the radial distribution
function, but by a 1D planar-averaged method. Specifically, the solution was divided
along the z-direction into slices at 3 Å intervals, and the number of OH- within each
slice was counted to generate a histogram of OH- distribution as a function of distance
along the z-axis. From this analysis, it was determined that the OH- count within 30 Å
of Pt-I was approximately half that observed near pristine Pt.
Comment 4: The MD simulations applied an external electric field of 0.2 V/Å along
the z-direction (as described in the Supplementary Information). How was this field
strength chosen, and does it reflect the experimental electrolysis conditions?
Response: The field strength was chosen based on the interfacial electric field during
HER, corresponding to 100 mA cm-2 (overpotential ~465 mV). It was applied along the
z-direction (normal to the electrode surface) to simulate cathodic polarization. This
enhanced repulsion from the negatively charged surface (synergistic with the I- charge)
and accelerated OH- diffusion into the bulk electrolyte.
Comment 5: Were MD simulations also conducted for other halogen-modified surfaces
(Pt–F, Pt–Cl, Pt–Br)? If so, how did their OH⁻ exclusion behaviors compare with Pt–
I? If not, could the trend in halogen electronegativity (F > Cl > Br > I) provide
mechanistic insight into the unique supersolidophobicity observed for Pt–I?
Response: MD simulations were performed only for Pt–I (Fig. 4d-f, Supplementary
Figure 47). The electronegativity trend is F (4.000) > Cl (3.475) > Br (3.219) > I (2.778),
where lower electronegativity indicates a stronger anionic character1. Accordingly, I-
retains more negative charge, resulting in stronger repulsion of OH-.
This
electronegativity trend is consistent with the experimentally observed order of stability
and solidophobicity: Pt-I > Pt-Br > Pt-Cl > Pt-F (Fig. 3b and 4b, Supplementary Figure
42). Therefore, while all halogen-coordinated samples exhibit solidophobic
characteristics, Pt–I demonstrates a supersolidophobic behavior.

Response: To achieve a greener and more sustainable future, reducing reliance on
precious metals is essential6. With the development of various catalysts, many
inexpensive metals have shown strong catalytic performance and can, to some extent,
serve as alternatives to precious metal catalysts. However, considering only earth-
abundant metals (inexpensive metals) as substitutes for precious metals is insufficient
to make catalysis greener and more sustainable7. Although inexpensive metals
generally have lower environmental impacts (e.g., global warming potential,
cumulative energy demand, and terrestrial acidification) than precious metals such as
Pt and Ir, precious metal catalysts offer advantages in terms of longer lifetimes, lower
maintenance costs, and easier scalability, which can effectively reduce overall
environmental impact8-12. Furthermore, while deactivation of precious metals during
electrocatalytic reactions can often be mitigated through regeneration13, the
deactivation of inexpensive metals is usually accompanied by dissolution or similar
processes, making regeneration more difficult14,15. Therefore, although precious metals
are used in the reaction, advanced recycling and regeneration technologies can further
mitigate their environmental impact16. In addition, with learning effects, economies of
scale, and the widespread adoption of renewable energy in the future17,18, the
environmental footprint of seawater electrolysis with hydrogen production and
magnesium extraction system will be further reduced, while its economic benefits will
continue to improve.

Response: In response to the reviewer’s comments, we have conducted a Life Cycle
Assessment (LCA) of the environmental impact of the seawater electrolysis-based
magnesium extraction and hydrogen production process using the Simapro. Further
details are provided in the Supplementary Information. Due to the advantages of noble
metal catalysts, such as longer lifespan, lower maintenance costs, and easier
scalability8-12, they can effectively reduce the overall environmental impact.
Furthermore, during electrocatalytic reactions, the deactivation of noble metals can
typically be mitigated through regeneration13, extending their lifespan and
compensating for the environmental impact associated with their extraction and
processing. Therefore, in the LCA analysis, the environmental impact of the catalyst
component was not considered for any hydrogen production system. As shown in
Figure R21 and Table R1, we compared the environmental impacts of hydrogen
produced by seawater electrolysis–based magnesium extraction under green electricity
and conventional electricity with those of commercial hydrogen. Even when powered
by conventional electricity, the key indicators GWP and ADP remain lower than those
of commercial hydrogen. Additionally, in response to the reviewer’s comments, we
have incorporated the LCA analysis into the main text, as shown in Fig. 5f. We
therefore conclude that leveraging the locally generated alkaline environment at the
cathode during seawater electrolysis to precipitate Mg2+ offers an effective alternative
to conventional, high-impact Mg(OH) production methods while simultaneously
2
coupling green hydrogen production. This “double-product” strategy advantage can
substantially reduce the overall environmental impact.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
Dear authors,
I am pleased to see the improvements made to the manuscript and the inclusion of LCA work, which has the potential to significantly enhance the quality of the paper by demonstrating the sustainability of the technology in terms of its technical capabilities, economic feasibility, and environmental performance. Most of the previous comments have been addressed appropriately. However, two major aspects still require improvement: (1) the sensitivity analysis and (2), in particular, the LCA. Further details are provided in the comments below.
IMPORTANT: It is essential that the sensitivity analysis and the LCA are presented with the highest level of transparency. At present, some of the reported calculations appear questionable, either due to insufficient description of the methodology or potential errors in the calculations themselves. For the next revision, please ensure that any errors are corrected and/or that the calculation methodology is described in sufficient detail to enable reproducibility and proper verification.
MANUSCRIPT
Abstract
Line 38-40: The authors performed a life cycle assessment. Hence, I would also mention it in the abstract.
Main Body:
Line 257: Fig. 5:
o For Fig. 5e: If possible, highlight the margin between costs and benefits as potential “profits”. By doing this, it will be clear to the reader that it is economically profitable just by looking at Figure 5e.
o Fig. 5f: While it shows the relative comparison between two alternatives, the magnitude is not evident here. The scale goes from 15 to -15. What exactly does it mean? For the mid-point impact categories abbreviation, I would write down the full meaning of it in the caption, or refer to the supplementary material where it is fully written down.
Line 300-309: Instead of listing the different categories, I would rather discuss the outcome in comparison to the conventional H2 production. I would move the categories in the supplementary material. Listing up the impact factor categories without any context in the main text seems to be unprofessional.
MANUSCRIPT/SUPPLEMENTAL MATERIAL:
The most crucial aspect is the performed LCA. While the reviewer greatly appreciates the effort put into this analysis and fully acknowledges its importance, there are several critical points that must be (i) addressed, (ii) revised, and (iii) checked before the work can be considered for publication.
(1) The absence of the catalyst from the assessment may lead to a substantial underestimation of the environmental impacts. In particular, assumptions regarding catalyst lifespan, regeneration potential, and low maintenance costs remain insufficiently substantiated, as they are primarily based on laboratory-scale results. The suggested study (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0101298) demonstrates that the GHG emissions of iridium and platinum are immense. While it is understood that modelling the catalyst’s contribution may be challenging, this aspect should be addressed at a minimum through a dedicated discussion in the main text or supplementary material. At present, it is mentioned solely in the rebuttal and not incorporated into the manuscript or supplementary files. The omission of such a discussion risks undermining the credibility of the LCA, especially among LCA experts.
(2) Unfortunately, the manuscript does not yet include essential elements that constitute the minimum requirements for a robust and publishable LCA:
o What is the functional unit?
o What are the system boundaries?
o Does your LCA align with the ISO 14044?
o What approach has been used to define your system boundaries (e.g. cradle-to-gate or grave-to-grave, etc.)
o What LCA approach has been used? (consequential or attributional)?
o What allocation method has been used as you have a multi-product process? (e.g. Economic, mass allocation, or system expansion, see ISO 14040).
o What LCIA (life cycle impact assessment) method has been used? It is indicated in SimaPro.
(3) Line 761-771, Supplementary material: While the improvement from average H2 production (I) to electrolysing seawater for hydrogen production using conventional electricity (III) seems to be reasonable and consistent with the described technology, the reported improvement from (III) to (II = seawater for hydrogen production using green electricity) remains highly questionable. The negative values, representing beneficial contributions (e.g., carbon sinks), appear to result solely from the assumed use of green electricity. However, it is difficult to reconcile this with the implication that the technology becomes a net carbon sink from a GWP/greenhouse gas emissions perspective. The same applies to all other indicators reported as negative. For instance, even when renewable energy is used, greenhouse gas emissions (kg CO₂-eq.) are still generated, which also holds true across all other impact categories:
ReCiPe2016 from SimaPro:
- Green electricity in Germany (kg CO2-eq/kWh)
• Photovoltaic: 0.0981
• Wind: 0.0073
• Nuclear: 0.00653 (debatable if green or not)
- Green electricity in China (kg CO2-eq/kWh)
• Photovoltaic: 0.0785
• Wind: 0.049
• Nuclear: 0.000783
- Average conventional electricity mixes (including different national-based electricity sources) (kg CO2-eq/kWh) in…,
• China: 1.26.
• World: 0.861.
• USA: 0.577.
=> Hence, it is highly unlikely that the use of green electricity alone would render the technology a net (carbon) sink. This outcome suggests either a significant error in the LCA calculation/modelling or the presence of another factor that has not been sufficiently explained. It is therefore essential to correct and/or provide a detailed elaboration of this result, as the current information is insufficient to verify the LCI and LCA. Transparency and comprehensive explanation are critical in LCA studies, particularly when certain information must remain confidential.
SUPPLEMENTAL MATERIAL (referring to figures and text that have been included)
(1)Sensitivity analysis: Fig. 66, line 725:
Fig. 66a: correct.
Fig. 66b: almost the same results. Probably due to different digits after the comma.
According to the reviewer’s calculation: Sensitivity analysis: NaOH:
• 10% higher = 1.209 USD/kg H2
•-10% -= still positive = 0.09 USD/kg H2
=> For both 66a and b: Discuss and explain what implications the negative outcomes have for your technology and economic feasibility.
Fig. 66c: correct
Fig. 66d: seems to be incorrect, or the calculation approach is not sufficiently described to be followed. Please make sure that the calculation way and method is transparent enough to reproduce the numbers/outcome.
REBUTTAL part:
(1)Sensitivity analysis: Electrolyser (page 46-487):
o The sensitivity analysis for the electrolyser seems to be off, given the calculation method that has been provided by lines 256-257, lines 288-289, and line 292 in the supplementary materials.
o Taking a price of USD 2500/kW (as indicated in the rebuttal) and US electricity price of 0.1331 USD/kWh, the hydrogen cost rises to approx. 11.76 USD/ kg H2. Even if the electricity price is kept constant (based on the benchmark of 0.03 USD/kWh), the outcome would still be higher than calculated, which is 8.42 USD/ kg H2.
o Correct this mistake and provide a transparent and detailed calculation.
(2) Sensitivity: Electricity price (Page 48):
o The calculation seems to have an error. The benchmark electricity price is USD 0.03/kWh, and the Finnish electricity price is 0.067 EUR/kWh (= 0.07906 USD/kWh => more than double). Hence, it is not possible that the Finnish electricity price will lead to a negative hydrogen production cost (or decrease => it must increase). According to line 262 in the supplementary material: Electricity: 315.85 kW x 24h/day USD 0.079/kWh x (day/0.1 ton) = USD 5992 per ton H2. => 4.33 USD/kg H2. The same issues apply to the other electricity prices. Hence, there must be a calculating error. Please correct it.

Response: We fully agree with the reviewer that the environmental impacts associated
with the use of catalysts should not be overlooked. Accordingly, based on the catalyst
lifetime and loading obtained from our laboratory stability tests, as well as the
environmental impact data for platinum and iridium reported in the ecoinvent 3.11
database and previous studies (DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0101298), we reanalyzed the
environmental impacts of the seawater electrolysis-based magnesium extraction and
hydrogen production process (Table R1 and R2). According to the assumptions for
industrial-scale production described in the Supplementary Information, under an
electrode area of 112 m2 and a current density of 100 mA cm-2, the production of 1 t of

environmental impact assessment.

(2) Unfortunately, the manuscript does not yet include essential elements that
constitute the minimum requirements for a robust and publishable LCA:
o What is the functional unit?
o What are the system boundaries?
o Does your LCA align with the ISO 14044?
o What approach has been used to define your system boundaries (e.g. cradle-to-
gate or grave-to-grave, etc.)
o What LCA approach has been used? (consequential or attributional)?
o What allocation method has been used as you have a multi-product process?
(e.g. Economic, mass allocation, or system expansion, see ISO 14040).
o What LCIA (life cycle impact assessment) method has been used? It is indicated
in SimaPro.
Response: In our manuscript, the production of 1 t of hydrogen was defined as the
functional unit, and the system boundary was set on a cradle-to-gate basis. The
boundary mainly includes the production processes of hydrogen and magnesium
hydroxide in the seawater electrolysis-based magnesium extraction and hydrogen
production process. The environmental impact assessment follows the international
standard ISO 14044. Furthermore, a system expansion approach was adopted for the
attributional LCA, assuming that the co-produced byproduct could substitute
conventionally produced materials in the market and thus generate environmental
benefits. All analyses were conducted using the CML 2001 method, in which the
characterization results quantify the specific contributions of various environmental
impact categories (AP, GWP, FAETP, MAETP, TETP, ADP, EP, HTP, ADP element,
ODP, and POCP) to represent the overall life-cycle environmental impacts. The
Supplementary Information has been revised to provide a more comprehensive
explanation of the environmental impact assessment methodology.
Revision in the revised Supplementary Information:
LCA analysis. An LCA was conducted using the SimaPro software following the
international standard ISO 14040. The CML 2001 method was selected to evaluate the
environmental impacts of the studied system, and background data were obtained from
the Ecoinvent 3.11 database. The production of 1 t of hydrogen was defined as the
functional unit, and the system boundary was set on a cradle-to-gate basis, covering the
production processes of hydrogen and magnesium hydroxide in the seawater
electrolysis-based magnesium extraction and hydrogen production process. A life-cycle
inventory was established to clearly distinguish the system inputs and outputs. The main
inputs include seawater, sodium hydroxide, catalyst materials, and electricity, while the
outputs consist of hydrogen, oxygen, and magnesium hydroxide. A system expansion
approach was applied for the attributional LCA, assuming that the co-produced
byproducts could substitute conventionally produced materials in the market and
thereby generate environmental benefits. Based on the CML 2001 method, the
characterization analysis quantified the specific contributions of each environmental
impact category (AP, GWP, FAETP, MAETP, TETP, ADP, EP, HTP, ADP element,
ODP, and POCP) to represent the overall life-cycle environmental impacts.

in CO emissions, leading to questions regarding how the seawater electrolysis-based
2
magnesium extraction and hydrogen production process can achieve carbon sinks. It
should be noted that, in this study, a system expansion approach was adopted, assuming
